title: Where Music, Patterns, Math, Chemistry and Physics Meet
license: CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook; credit + link back required

regions.title: Scales: the ladders music climbs
regions.intro: A scale is a pattern of whole and half steps. Keep the pattern, start on any key, and the tune sounds the same, only higher or lower.

regions.title: Times tables on a circle
regions.intro: Put numbers around a circle, join each one to its double, and a heart shape appears. The math is clock arithmetic.

regions.title: Star patterns from simple tiles
regions.intro: The interlaced stars on mosque walls and tiled floors can be drawn from a plain grid of polygons, with one angle you choose.

regions.title: The periodic table, by block
regions.intro: Color the periodic table by which kind of subshell each element is filling, and its odd shape makes sense: blocks 2, 6, 10 and 14 wide.

regions.title: What stays the same
regions.intro: Physics looks for the things that do not change while everything else does. A swinging pendulum trades height for speed and back again, and the total never moves.

regions.title: Ratios, clocks and rhythms
regions.intro: Notes that sound good together have frequencies in simple whole-number ratios. Scales are clock arithmetic, and some of the world’s favorite rhythms come from an algorithm Euclid wrote down about 2,300 years ago.

regions.title: Sand that draws sound
regions.intro: Sprinkle sand on a metal plate, make it ring, and the sand jumps into a pattern. Tunes have mirror images too: composers flip and reverse melodies the way artists flip a design.

regions.title: Octaves of elements, notes of molecules
regions.intro: In 1865 a chemist compared the elements to a musical scale and was laughed at. He was on to something. And molecules do have “notes” of a sort: they vibrate, much too fast to hear.

regions.title: Tilings and rose windows
regions.intro: Every repeating wallpaper follows one of just 17 sets of rules, and a cathedral’s rose window can be drawn with nothing but a compass and a straightedge.

regions.title: The numbers behind the periodic table
regions.intro: Why the table’s rows hold 2, 8, 18 and 32 elements, and how balancing a chemical equation is a problem in linear algebra.

regions.title: Crystals, snowflakes and stained glass
regions.intro: Atoms stack in repeating patterns that sort into seven families, and a pinch of metal in molten glass gives a cathedral window its blues and reds.

regions.title: Sound is a wave in the air
regions.intro: A note is air pressure rising and falling hundreds of times a second. Play two notes that are almost the same and you can hear the waves themselves slide in and out of step.

regions.title: Kepler's ellipse
regions.intro: For two thousand years astronomers built the sky out of circles. In 1609 Johannes Kepler found that a planet’s path is an ellipse, and three short laws replaced all the circles.

regions.title: Stripes made of light
regions.intro: Shine light through two narrow slits and you do not get two bright lines. You get a row of stripes. The pattern settled an old argument about what light is.

regions.title: The atom as a small solar system
regions.intro: In 1913 Niels Bohr pictured the hydrogen atom as an electron circling a proton, held by the same kind of force that holds a planet. The picture was wrong in its details and right about the energies.

regions.title: A sound built from harmonics
regions.intro: Every steady musical tone is a stack of simple waves at 1, 2, 3, 4 … times its pitch. Change the stack and the same note turns into a flute, a clarinet or a buzz.

regions.title: Hydrogen's whole-number lines
regions.intro: In 1885 a schoolteacher found a whole-number formula for the colors of light that hydrogen gives off. It looks a little like the harmonic series, and the difference turned out to matter enormously.

regions.title: Vibrating plates and orbital shapes
regions.intro: The sand patterns on a ringing plate and the shapes of electron orbitals are both maps of standing waves. Count the still lines and circles, and they match.

regions.title: The symmetry of molecules
regions.intro: Turn a benzene ring by a sixth of a circle and it looks exactly the same. Chemists count these moves, and the count tells them how a molecule behaves.

regions.title: Moons that keep time
regions.intro: Three of Jupiter’s moons go round in the ratio 4 to 2 to 1, like three drummers playing in strict time. A continued fraction can tell which pairs in the sky are locked like that and which are not.

regions.title: Gaps carved by rhythm
regions.intro: Resonance can also empty a place. The asteroid belt has gaps where an asteroid would keep simple time with Jupiter, and Saturn’s rings have an edge where a ring particle would keep time with a moon.

regions.title: An atom a radio can hear
regions.intro: In the thin gas between the stars, an atom’s electron can orbit so far out that the atom is a tenth of a millimeter wide. A radio telescope picks up the fourth harmonic of that electron’s orbit.

regions.title: Order that survives, order that breaks
regions.intro: Give a regular motion a small regular kick. Some of its smooth curves survive and some break into chaos. Which ones survive depends on how well a single number can be matched by fractions.

regions.title: Why the periodic table has its shape
regions.intro: The shells of an atom hold 2, 8, 18 and 32 electrons. Those numbers come from a symmetry of the inverse-square force, the same symmetry that keeps a planet’s ellipse from swinging round.

regions.title: Seeing atoms with X-rays
regions.intro: A crystal is too small to see, but X-rays bounced off its layers of atoms make a pattern of spots. From the spots, people worked out the structure of salt, of diamond and of DNA.

regions.title: Waves and symmetry
regions.intro: The center of the diagram: a drum, a cathedral window, a snowflake and the periodic table all come from waves and symmetry. An atom’s orbitals are three-dimensional standing waves, like the vibrations of a drum.

regions.title: Kepler's figures in the sky
regions.intro: Mark where two planets meet, again and again, and the marks draw a figure: a triangle for Jupiter and Saturn, a five-pointed star for Venus and the Earth. Kepler drew the first one in 1595, and looked in the planets for music.

regions.title: Orbits whose shapes are fractions
regions.intro: Kepler said a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. In the atom, Bohr allowed that sweep only in whole-number steps, and Sommerfeld’s ellipses had shapes given by simple fractions.

regions.title: Sound inside a crystal
regions.intro: The atoms of a crystal are joined as if by tiny springs. A push at one end travels through as a wave, and the whole crystal has notes it can ring at, like a string made of beads.

regions.title: Whole numbers a laboratory can measure
regions.intro: Electrons in a thin layer of crystal, in a strong magnetic field, conduct electricity in exact whole-number steps. The whole numbers come from Euclid’s algorithm, and the picture behind them is a fractal butterfly.

regions.title: One wave, five faces
regions.intro: At the center of the diagram is a single idea: a wave that has to fit. Fitting gives whole numbers, and the whole numbers show up as notes, as patterns, as energy levels and as orbits.
